claims.text: The investigated alloy has nominal composition Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in atomic percent.
The alloy was vacuum-arc melted, cast, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h under Ar, hot-forged, re-homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, and water-quenched.
The high-temperature state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is disordered BCC.
Rapid cooling from the high-temperature disordered BCC state causes spinodal decomposition within a miscibility gap.
The spinodal decomposition produces Ni–Al-lean BCC1 domains and Ni–Al-rich BCC2 domains.
On further cooling below an ordering transition, the Ni–Al-rich BCC domains order into B2 precipitates.
The resulting microstructure consists of a Ni–Al-lean BCC matrix containing Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 precipitates.
Higher annealing temperatures increase the density and scale of B2 precipitates.
Spinodal compositional modulations and ordered B2 domains increase the density of phase boundaries.
The phase boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion raises the alloy hardness.
The 1100 °C annealed and water-quenched baseline has a near-equal mixture of BCC and FCC phases.
The 1100 °C annealed and water-quenched condition has the lowest measured hardness among the compared conditions.
Relative to the 1100 °C baseline, specimens quenched from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will have a larger BCC phase fraction.
Relative to the 1100 °C baseline, specimens quenched from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will show more pronounced spinodal-decomposition features.
Relative to the 1100 °C baseline, specimens quenched from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will contain a higher density of ordered B2 precipitates.
Specimens quenched from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will be harder than the 1100 °C baseline because of the increased BCC/B2 boundary population.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under substantially slower cooling or when lower-temperature annealing produces predominantly FCC phase mixtures.
Current STEM–EDS compositional resolution limits precise characterization of the proposed nanoscale sequential decomposition.
